extracted.intended_audience: people who pitch stories to newsrooms (PR pros, nonprofit communicators, spokespeople, entrepreneurs, journalists learning story selection)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for developing and evaluating story pitches so they will be treated as news by journalists, with eight concrete news values to aim for. Useful for anyone trying to get press or television coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact
rubrics_metrics.description: How many people are affected by this story? The more, the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think about the difference between closing a side street or shutting down the 405 — one is news, one isn’t. Pitch stories that affect large numbers of people or have measurable consequences. (Salton Sea example: thousands of acres of exposed lakebed containing toxic dust subjecting nearby communities to health issues.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: When did the news happen? The sooner, the better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame what is new about the story today and how you can advance it. Newsrooms value immediacy (the author notes striving to have today's day of the week in every lead). Tie the pitch to current events, legislation, or an unfolding development. (Salton Sea example: federal legislation currently working through Congress, with an expected update soon.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Proximity
rubrics_metrics.description: Where is the story located? The closer it is, the more interesting it becomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local relevance increases newsworthiness for local outlets. If the subject is within the outlet's coverage area, emphasize that closeness. (Salton Sea: within the paper's coverage area.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prominence
rubrics_metrics.description: How prominent are the players in the story?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stories involving well-known people, institutions, or officials are more likely to get coverage (example: a bike crash becomes big news when the city's mayor is involved). Emphasize recognizable names or influential organizations in your pitch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rarity
rubrics_metrics.description: How unexpected are the elements of the story? Is this something special or out of the ordinary?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame unusual developments, rare events, or significant departures from the norm. Provide context to show how uncommon the event is (Salton Sea example: a 20-fold increase in funding after 30 years of research — presented as out of the ordinary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Currency
rubrics_metrics.description: Is this pitch about something we’re already covering? Is it part of a trend or larger conversation?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Connect the story to an ongoing beat, trend, or prior reporting to demonstrate how it builds out coverage or provides a useful sidebar. News leads to more news — show how your pitch advances or ties into existing reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposing forces make a story more compelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Highlight disagreements, controversies, policy fights, or legal battles. Show stakes and opposition (Salton Sea example: partisan votes and uncertainty in the Senate). Conflict often creates drama and editorial interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Can you put a face to this story? People care about other people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add human elements, personal stories, or identifiable individuals to make abstract issues relatable. A face, a local resident, or a personal anecdote can turn otherwise dry material into compelling television or feature copy.
